name: L-Carnitine
lead: L-carnitine is the biologically active form of carnitine, a quaternary ammonium compound made from amino acids that carries long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria so they can be burned for energy. It is concentrated in skeletal and cardiac muscle, and the body stores roughly 20 g of it, nearly all in muscle [1]. People take it in capsules, powders, drinks and, in some forum posts, injectable form, with the aim of leaner body composition, better training recovery and more muscle through more training [1][4][7].

Healthy people, including strict vegetarians, generally make enough in the body from lysine, and the compound was first extracted from meat in 1905, which gave it its name from the Latin for flesh [1]. Supplementary use is common among athletes and dieters, but Wikipedia states that clinical research quality for fat loss and performance uses is low [1]. A 2020 meta-analysis of 37 randomized trials with 2,292 participants reported small average reductions in body weight, body mass index and fat mass [2].

Carnitine is also a research subject in other areas: gut-bacteria-derived trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a compound linked in observational and animal work to cardiovascular risk [3][28][29]; muscle carnitine loading with insulin or carbohydrate [27]; and the FDA-approved prescription form levocarnitine, used in deficiency states [1]. Related forms sold as supplements include acetyl-L-carnitine and L-carnitine L-tartrate [15][25].

chain: Carnitine moves fatty acids into mitochondria

angle.text: Lifters and dieters take L-carnitine hoping to burn more fat and recover faster so they can train more. Meta-analyses report small average reductions in weight and fat mass, and reviews describe lower soreness markers after exercise.

paras: Because carnitine transports fatty acids into mitochondria, supplements are promoted for fat loss, for exercise performance and for recovery. T Nation users list it in pre-workout stacks, in competition-prep supplement lists and, in some posts, as an injected product; others describe it as helpful during thyroid-related fatigue or ask about it as a general aid [4][5][6][7][8].

Wikipedia notes that athletes commonly take it for performance and recovery, and that high-quality evidence of benefit is insufficient, and that it does not appear to aid weight loss [1]. The appearance chain proponents describe runs from more fat oxidation to lower body fat, and from less soreness to more training volume and muscle.

Carnitine supplementation is used for primary carnitine deficiency, a genetic transporter disorder, and for secondary deficiencies such as those in chronic kidney disease and in preterm infants [1]. The FDA approved levocarnitine (Carnitor) in 1985 for certain deficiency syndromes [1]. Trials have also examined it in diabetic kidney disease, spinal muscular atrophy (with valproic acid), cancer-related fatigue and pressure ulcers, with guideline bodies reaching their own conclusions in each setting [9][10][11][12]. Wikipedia reports that seminal carnitine levels correlate with sperm count and motility [1].

sections.h: Dietary sources and the body's own supply
paras: Most dietary carnitine comes from animal foods, especially red meat. Wikipedia gives omnivore intake as roughly 23 to 135 mg daily versus about 10 to 12 mg for vegans, and body synthesis from lysine, mainly in liver, kidney and brain, needs vitamin C and iron [1]. Because the kidneys conserve carnitine, low-carnitine diets have little effect on total levels [1]. A review of vegan athletes by researchers who also study carnitine concluded that evidence does not show a vegan diet changes athletic performance or recovery [27].

Another finding concerns uptake: carnitine enters muscle through the OCTN2 transporter [23], and studies by Francis Stephens and colleagues report that taking carnitine with carbohydrate, which raises insulin, increases muscle carnitine content, which otherwise changes slowly [27].

Carnitine acyltransferases (CPT1, a translocase and CPT2) move long-chain fatty acids across the mitochondrial membrane for beta-oxidation. The entry step is a rate-limiting control point for fat oxidation, inhibited by malonyl-CoA when the liver is making fat and relieved when AMPK activation lowers malonyl-CoA during fasting or vigorous contraction [1]. Carnitine also buffers acetyl-CoA, removes acyl groups as acylcarnitines and has antioxidant activity [1][22].

Adults on mixed diets take in roughly 60 to 180 mg a day from food by one estimate, and the body synthesises roughly 11 to 34 mg daily. Between 54 and 86 percent of dietary carnitine is absorbed. Supplemental carnitine has a plasma half-life of about 17 hours, and uptake into tissue depends on OCTN2 [1][23]. A 2023 randomised crossover study of six healthy young adults found that caffeine co-ingestion lowered plasma carnitine by about 15 percent during an intravenous carnitine infusion, which the authors interpreted as increased clearance [17][30].

L-carnitine is the natural form; Wikipedia says D-carnitine is toxic because it inhibits the L-form [1]. Acetyl-L-carnitine, an acetylated form, is sold as a supplement and is broken down to carnitine in blood; Wikipedia describes research on neuropathy, depression and dementia with mixed results, and notes a half-life of about 29 to 36 hours [25]. L-carnitine L-tartrate is the form most used in sport studies [15][27].

The 2020 dose-response meta-analysis of 37 randomized trials reported that carnitine supplementation reduced body weight by about 1.2 kg on average, BMI by about 0.24 kg/m2 and fat mass by about 2.1 kg, with no significant effect on waist circumference or body-fat percentage; restricting the analysis to high-quality trials confirmed only the weight effect, and the dose-response relationship was non-linear [2][13].

For exercise, a 2018 review concluded that carnitine has been investigated as an ergogenic aid and that later studies point to benefits for recovery such as reduced muscle soreness and markers of muscle damage [14][31]. A 2023 narrative scoping review likewise concluded that supplementation could aid post-exercise recovery while noting that only two studies measured inflammation and oxidative damage together [31]. A 2021 trial of carnitine tartrate for five weeks in men and women examined exercise recovery [15]. Wikipedia cites a 2021 systematic review that found carnitine may improve high-intensity performance and recovery but called results inconclusive because regimens varied [1]. A 2006 randomized crossover trial in ten resistance-trained men found that three weeks of L-carnitine L-tartrate raised androgen receptor content before exercise [32].

A 2021 trial in older men randomised 14 participants to carnitine tartrate or placebo for 25 weeks; muscle total carnitine rose about 20 percent and whole-body fat oxidation during moderate exercise rose about 20 percent, with no change in insulin-stimulated glucose disposal [27]. A 2020 systematic review of 11 studies in healthy adults reported that carnitine with carbohydrate raised muscle carnitine, that supplementation increased muscle mass and exercise tolerance in centenarians but not muscle strength in older women, and that fasting plasma TMAO rose [27].
A 2024 meta-analysis addressed carnitine's effect on lipid profile in adults [16]. Registered trials have examined skeletal muscle mass among many other conditions [18].

Wikipedia reports that around 3 g daily can cause nausea, diarrhea and a fishy body odour, that seizures are possible in people with epilepsy, and that valproic acid, phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine and pivalate-conjugated antibiotics can lower carnitine levels [1].

In 2013 a Nature Medicine study led by Robert Koeth and Stanley Hazen reported that gut microbes metabolise dietary L-carnitine into trimethylamine, which the liver converts to TMAO, and that this pathway promoted atherosclerosis in mice. In 2,595 people undergoing cardiac evaluation, plasma carnitine predicted cardiovascular events only in those with concurrently high TMAO, and omnivores produced more TMAO than vegans or vegetarians after carnitine [3][28]. A 2019 Journal of Clinical Investigation study found more than 20-fold higher TMAO production after oral labelled carnitine in omnivores (n=40) than in vegans and vegetarians (n=32), with a Clostridiales bacterium converting the intermediate gamma-butyrobetaine to trimethylamine [29]. Wikipedia describes high TMAO as associated with higher cardiovascular events and mortality in cited meta-analyses without claiming causation [26]. Follow-up work examined TMAO in kidney disease and stroke populations, and a 2022 trial in hemodialysis patients tested whether a dietary fibre could lower TMAO [19][20][21]. The significance of supplemental carnitine for cardiovascular risk in people has therefore been an active research question.

In forum logs carnitine appears most often as one item among many supplements taken before training, including citrulline, beta-alanine and betaine, and in some cases alongside testosterone and growth hormone. Mentions of injectable carnitine appear in posts by users on testosterone replacement [5][6][7][8][24]. It is discussed mainly in bodybuilding and strength forums such as T Nation rather than as a face-specific product [4][5].

lore.intro: In strength-sport communities carnitine is treated as a routine pre-workout or fat-loss supplement, and some users inject it [5][6][7].

claims.claim: L-carnitine burns fat by shuttling fatty acids into mitochondria
claims.believers: Users take it before training or during prep and describe it as a fat-oxidation aid[7][8]
claims.experts: A 37-trial meta-analysis found modest average reductions in weight and fat mass but no significant change in body-fat percentage; Wikipedia describes the evidence base for fat and performance claims as low quality[1][2].

claims.claim: It improves exercise recovery and performance
claims.believers: Lifters include it in pre-workout stacks and report using it around training[5][7]
claims.experts: A 2018 review reports reductions in markers of muscle damage and soreness, while a 2021 review cited by Wikipedia judged results inconclusive[1][14].

claims.claim: Injected carnitine works better than oral
claims.believers: Some posters on testosterone therapy report using injectable carnitine and say oral is acceptable with food or carbohydrate[4][24]
claims.experts: No trial comparing injected and oral supplementation for body composition was identified in the reviewed literature.

claims.claim: Supplemental carnitine is harmless because it is a natural amino-acid derivative
claims.believers: It is widely regarded as a routine supplement in forum stacks[5]
claims.experts: Research reports that gut bacteria convert dietary carnitine to TMAO, which is associated with atherosclerosis in mice and cardiovascular risk markers in humans; the clinical relevance of supplementation is still under investigation[3].

claims.claim: Taking it with carbohydrate raises muscle carnitine and fat burning
claims.believers: Lifters take it alongside carbohydrate-containing meals [4][24].
claims.experts: Studies by Stephens and colleagues report that carnitine with carbohydrate raises muscle carnitine content and, over 25 weeks in older men, fat oxidation during exercise [27].

claims.claim: Caffeine combined with carnitine is a useful pairing
claims.believers: Pre-workout stack lists combine carnitine with stimulants [7].
claims.experts: A 2023 study of six adults found caffeine lowered plasma carnitine by about 15 percent during infusion; the authors suggest possible muscle loading strategies [17][30].
